claim: Without extracellular Ca2+, ER Ca2+ release is the source of intracellular Ca2+ oscillations induced by laser-tweezer-traction at the plasma membrane in human mesenchymal stem cells.
source: Without extracellular Ca2+, ER Ca2+ release is the source of intracellular Ca2+ oscillations induced by laser-tweezer-traction at the plasma membrane, providing a model to study how mechanical stimuli can be transmitted deep inside the cell body.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing Ca2+ oscillations in the absence of extracellular Ca2+, as described in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 1.

claim: ER Ca2+ release upon mechanical stimulation is mediated by the mechanical support of cytoskeleton.
source: This ER Ca2+ release upon mechanical stimulation is mediated not only by the mechanical support of cytoskeleton and actomyosin contractility, but also by mechanosensitive Ca2+ permeable channels on the plasma membrane, specifically TRPM7.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using cytoskeletal disruption agents (cytochalasin D and nocodazole) shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: ER Ca2+ release upon mechanical stimulation is mediated by actomyosin contractility.
source: This ER Ca2+ release upon mechanical stimulation is mediated not only by the mechanical support of cytoskeleton and actomyosin contractility, but also by mechanosensitive Ca2+ permeable channels on the plasma membrane, specifically TRPM7.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using ML-7 and blebbistatin to inhibit actomyosin contractility, shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: ER Ca2+ release upon mechanical stimulation is mediated by mechanosensitive Ca2+ permeable channels on the plasma membrane, specifically TRPM7.
source: This ER Ca2+ release upon mechanical stimulation is mediated not only by the mechanical support of cytoskeleton and actomyosin contractility, but also by mechanosensitive Ca2+ permeable channels on the plasma membrane, specifically TRPM7.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using TRPM7 siRNA knockdown shown in Figure 2E-F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ca2+ influx at the plasma membrane via mechanosensitive Ca2+ permeable channels is mediated by the passive cytoskeletal structure.
source: However, Ca2+ influx at the plasma membrane via mechanosensitive Ca2+ permeable channels is only mediated by the passive cytoskeletal structure but not active actomyosin contractility.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that cytoskeletal disruption inhibits Ca2+ influx (Figure 4C-D) while actomyosin contractility inhibition does not.

claim: Ca2+ influx at the plasma membrane via mechanosensitive Ca2+ permeable channels is not mediated by active actomyosin contractility.
source: However, Ca2+ influx at the plasma membrane via mechanosensitive Ca2+ permeable channels is only mediated by the passive cytoskeletal structure but not active actomyosin contractility.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that ML-7 and blebbistatin did not affect force-induced Ca2+ influx (Figure 4C-D).

claim: Active actomyosin contractility is essential for the response of ER to external mechanical stimuli.
source: Thus, active actomyosin contractility is essential for the response of ER to the external mechanical stimuli, distinct from the mechanical regulation at the plasma membrane.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that inhibition of actomyosin contractility abolished ER Ca2+ release (Figure 2C-D) but not plasma membrane Ca2+ influx (Figure 4C-D).

claim: Calcium ion (Ca2+) is involved in muscle contraction, differentiation, proliferation, gene expression, and apoptosis.
source: Calcium ion (Ca2+) as one of the most important biochemical signals, is involved in many cellular processes, including muscle contraction, differentiation, proliferation, gene expression, and apoptosis (Berridge et al., 2000; West et al., 2001; McKinsey et al., 2002; Landsberg and Yuan, 2004; Clapham, 2007; Maeda et al., 2007; Rong and Distelhorst, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Various mechanical stimulations can affect cytosolic Ca2+ signals as well as Ca2+ dynamics in organelles or subcellular compartments, such as mitochondria and focal adhesion sites.
source: Various mechanical stimulations can affect cytosolic Ca2+ signals as well as Ca2+ dynamics in organelles or subcellular compartments, such as mitochondria and focal adhesion sites (Balasubramanian et al., 2007; Belmonte and Morad, 2008; Hayakawa et al., 2008; Horner and Wolfner, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Most cells mobilize their Ca2+ signals via the Ca2+ entry across the plasma membrane and/or the Ca2+ release from intracellular stores such as endoplasmic reticulum (ER) or sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR).
source: Most cells mobilize their Ca2+ signals via the Ca2+ entry across the plasma membrane and/or the Ca2+ release from intracellular stores such as endoplasmic reticulum (ER) or sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) (Wehrens et al., 2005; Clapham, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) is known to regulate Ca2+ release from ER.
source: Biochemical signals, such as inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3), are known to regulate Ca2+ release from ER.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Direct regulation of ER Ca2+ signals by mechanical force is unknown.
source: But direct regulation of ER Ca2+ signals by mechanical force is unknown.
evidence: The claim represents a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: Human mesenchymal stem cells (HMSCs) display Ca2+ oscillations.
source: The human mesenchymal stem cells (HMSCs) displaying Ca2+ oscillations provide a model system to study that (Kawano et al., 2002; Sun et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Ca2+ influx at the plasma membrane and release from ER are the only two sources for Ca2+ oscillations in HMSCs.
source: As Ca2+ influx at the plasma membrane and release from ER are the only two sources for Ca2+ oscillations in HMSCs (Kawano et al., 2002; Kim et al., 2009), we dissected the effect of mechanical force on each process by monitoring the calcium signals at subcellular locations.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: When fibronectin (Fn)-coated beads were seeded onto the HMSCs and 300 pN of mechanical force was applied by optical laser tweezers, Ca2+ oscillations were induced in HMSCs.
source: When fibronectin (Fn)-coated beads were seeded onto the HMSCs and 300 pN of mechanical force was applied by optical laser tweezers as described previously (Wang et al., 2005), Ca2+ oscillations were induced in HMSCs (Figure 1C-F, Video 1) but not in bovine aortic endothelial cells (BAECs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-F and Video 1.

claim: Laser-tweezer-traction on fibronectin-coated beads did not induce Ca2+ oscillations in bovine aortic endothelial cells (BAECs).
source: When fibronectin (Fn)-coated beads were seeded onto the HMSCs and 300 pN of mechanical force was applied by optical laser tweezers as described previously (Wang et al., 2005), Ca2+ oscillations were induced in HMSCs (Figure 1C-F, Video 1) but not in bovine aortic endothelial cells (BAECs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Laser-tweezer-traction on bovine serum albumin (BSA)-coated beads did not cause any Ca2+ oscillations in HMSCs.
source: In contrast, laser-tweezer-traction on bovine serum albumin (BSA)-coated beads did not cause any oscillations (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-F.

claim: Without extracellular Ca2+, mechanical force can induce Ca2+ oscillations by triggering Ca2+ release from ER.
source: These results indicate that without extracellular Ca2+, mechanical force can induce Ca2+ oscillations by triggering Ca2+ release from ER.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing Ca2+ oscillations in the absence of extracellular Ca2+.

claim: Depletion of ER Ca2+ by Thapsigargin (TG) entirely abolished the force-induced oscillations.
source: Further experiments showed that depletion of ER Ca2+ by Thapsigargin (TG) or inhibition of Ca2+ release from the ER by 2-Amino-ethoxydiphenylborate (2-APB) entirely abolished the force-induced oscillations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Inhibition of Ca2+ release from the ER by 2-Amino-ethoxydiphenylborate (2-APB) entirely abolished the force-induced oscillations.
source: Further experiments showed that depletion of ER Ca2+ by Thapsigargin (TG) or inhibition of Ca2+ release from the ER by 2-Amino-ethoxydiphenylborate (2-APB) entirely abolished the force-induced oscillations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The ER Ca2+ store is the main source for the force-induced oscillations in HMSCs without extracellular Ca2+.
source: These results confirmed that the ER Ca2+ store is the main source for the force-induced oscillations in HMSCs without extracellular Ca2+.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results with TG and 2-APB.

claim: Mechanical force did not induce any change of IP3 in HMSCs.
source: Mechanical force did not induce any change of IP3 while ATP increased IP3 production in HMSCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that the second mechanism is unlikely.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using a FRET-based IP3 biosensor shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: ATP increased IP3 production in HMSCs.
source: Mechanical force did not induce any change of IP3 while ATP increased IP3 production in HMSCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that the second mechanism is unlikely.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Laser-tweezer-traction transmits deep inside the cells to mechanically release Ca2+ from ER.
source: Therefore, laser-tweezer-traction should transmit deep inside the cells to mechanically release Ca2+ from ER.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mechanical force induces ER Ca2+ release without IP3 production.

claim: Cytoskeleton is known to transmit mechanical forces and conduct mechanotransduction.
source: Cytoskeleton is known to transmit mechanical forces and conduct mechanotransduction (Hamill and Martinac, 2001; Orr et al., 2006; Schwartz and DeSimone, 2008), so we investigated the role of cytoskeleton and its associated proteins in the force-induced ER Ca2+ release.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The disruption of cytoskeletal actin filaments by cytochalasin D (Cyto D) completely eliminated the force-induced Ca2+ oscillations.
source: The disruption of cytoskeletal actin filaments by cytochalasin D (Cyto D) or microtubules by nocodazole (Noc) completely eliminated the force-induced Ca2+ oscillations (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The disruption of microtubules by nocodazole (Noc) completely eliminated the force-induced Ca2+ oscillations.
source: The disruption of cytoskeletal actin filaments by cytochalasin D (Cyto D) or microtubules by nocodazole (Noc) completely eliminated the force-induced Ca2+ oscillations (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The inhibition of actomyosin contractility by ML-7 completely eliminated the force-induced Ca2+ oscillations.
source: In addition, the inhibition of actomyosin contractility by ML-7 or blebbistatin had the same effect (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The inhibition of actomyosin contractility by blebbistatin completely eliminated the force-induced Ca2+ oscillations.
source: In addition, the inhibition of actomyosin contractility by ML-7 or blebbistatin had the same effect (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The deep penetration and transmission of force inside the cell and the induction of Ca2+ release from ER depend on both cytoskeletal support and actomyosin contractility.
source: Thus, the deep penetration and transmission of force inside the cell and the induction of Ca2+ release from ER depend on both cytoskeletal support and actomyosin contractility.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that disruption of cytoskeleton or inhibition of actomyosin contractility eliminates force-induced ER Ca2+ release.

claim: Long-distance force propagation to the deep cytoplasm depends on cytoskeleton tension.
